{{Short description|Eight-dimensional Riemannian manifold}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Spin(7)-manifold''' is an eight-dimensional [[Riemannian manifold]] whose [[holonomy group]] is contained in [[Spin group|Spin(7)]]. Spin(7)-manifolds are [[Ricci-flat]] and admit a parallel [[spinor]].  They also admit a parallel 4-[[Differential form|form]], known as the Cayley form, which is a [[calibrated geometry|calibrating form]] for a special class of submanifolds called Cayley cycles.  In fact, the Riemannian metric and the Cayley form determine each other.

==History==
The fact that Spin(7) might possibly arise as the holonomy group of certain Riemannian 8-manifolds was first suggested by the 1955 [[classification theorem]] of [[Marcel Berger]], and this possibility remained consistent with the simplified proof of Berger's theorem given by [[James Harris Simons|Jim Simons]] in 1962. Although not a single example of such a manifold had yet been discovered, [[Edmond Bonan]] then showed in 1966 that, if such a manifold did in fact exist, it would carry a parallel 4-form, and that it would necessarily be Ricci-flat.<ref>{{cite journal | first = Edmond| last =Bonan |author-link=Edmond Bonan| title = Sur les variétés riemanniennes à groupe d'holonomie G<sub>2</sub> ou Spin(7)| journal = [[Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences|C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris]] | volume =262| year = 1966  | pages = 127&ndash;129 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k6236863n/f141.item}}</ref> The first local examples of 8-manifolds with holonomy Spin(7) were finally constructed around 1984 by [[Robert Bryant (mathematician)|Robert Bryant]], and his full proof of their existence appeared in the [[Annals of Mathematics]] in 1987.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bryant |first1=Robert L. |author-link1=Robert Bryant (mathematician) |title=Metrics with exceptional holonomy |journal=[[The Annals of Mathematics]] |date=November 1987 |volume=126 |issue=3 |pages=525–576 |doi=10.2307/1971360 |jstor=1971360 }}</ref> Next, complete (but still noncompact) 8-manifolds with holonomy Spin(7) were explicitly constructed by Bryant and S. Salamon in 1989.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bryant |first1=Robert L. |author-link1=Robert Bryant (mathematician) |last2=Salamon |first2=Simon M. |title=On the construction of some complete metrics with exceptional holonomy |journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]] |date=1 June 1989 |volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=829–850 |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-89-05839-0}}</ref> The first examples of [[compact manifold|compact]] Spin(7)-manifolds were then constructed by [[Dominic Joyce]] in 1996.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Joyce |first1=D. D. |author-link1=Dominic Joyce |title=Compact 8-manifolds with holonomy Spin(7) |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |date=September 1996 |volume=123 |issue=3 |pages=507–552 |doi=10.1007/s002220050039}}</ref>

== Equivalent definition ==
By definition, a Spin(7)-manifold is a Riemannian manifold with Spin(7) holonomy.  However, it is generally easier to work with an equivalent definition based on the existence of a Cayley form: a differential form with certain properties.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Salamon |first1=Dietmar A. |author-link1=Dietmar Salamon |title=Notes on the octonions |date=2017-04-06 |eprint=1005.2820 |last2=Walpuski |first2=Thomas |class=math.RA }}</ref>

There are multiple equivalent ways of defining a Cayley form on an 8-manifold ''X''. The most succinct is the following.
{{block indent|A '''Cayley form''' is a 4-form <math>\Phi\in\Omega^4(X)</math> such that at each point <math>p\in X</math>, the [[Stabilizer (group theory)|stabilizer]] of <math>\Phi|_p</math> is Spin(7).}}
We also require a notion of positivity.  Given a vector ''v'' and a form <math>\omega</math>, let <math>\iota_v\omega</math> denote the [[interior product]].
{{block indent|A Cayley form <math>\Phi\in\Omega^4(X)</math> is called '''positive''' if the [[Volume form|top-dimensional forms]] <math>\Phi\wedge\Phi</math> and <math>\iota_v\iota_u\Phi\wedge\iota_v\iota_u\Phi\wedge\Phi</math> induce the same [[Orientability|orientation]] whenever ''u'' and ''v'' are linearly independent. It is called '''negative''' if it is not positive.}}

With the above established, one can define a Spin(7)-structure.
{{block indent|Let <math>X</math> be a smooth 8-manifold. A '''Spin(7)-structure''' on <math>X</math> is a 4-form <math>\Phi\in\Omega^4(X)</math> which restricts to a positive Cayley form on each [[tangent space]].  In this case, the pair <math>(X,\Phi)</math> is called an '''almost Spin(7) manifold'''. An almost Spin(7) manifold <math>(X,\Phi)</math> is called a '''Spin(7)-manifold''' if <math>\Phi</math> is [[closed and exact differential forms|closed]].}}

It turns out that every almost Spin(7) manifold admits a Riemannian metric which is ''compatible'' with <math>\Phi</math> in the sense that
<math display="block">\iota_v\iota_u\Phi\wedge\iota_v\iota_u\Phi\wedge\Phi = 6|u\wedge v|^2\operatorname{vol}</math>
for any pair of vectors ''v'' and ''u''.  When <math>\Phi</math> is closed, this metric has Spin(7) holonomy.

One can also explicitly construct the metric determined by the Cayley form via Karigiannis's formula.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Karigiannis |first=Spiro |date=2005-10-01 |title=Deformations of G 2 and Spin(7) Structures |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0008414X00023415/type/journal_article |journal=Canadian Journal of Mathematics |language=en |volume=57 |issue=5 |pages=1012–1055 |arxiv=math/0301218 |doi=10.4153/CJM-2005-039-x |issn=0008-414X}}</ref> The metric is defined up to scaling of the Cayley form.
